chunks: What back EMF is. The question: What is back EMF?
Back-EMF is the voltage a motor generates simply because it is spinning. A motor and a generator are the same device.
When the shaft turns, the coil moving through a magnetic field makes a voltage. In a motor, that voltage pushes against the supply, which is why it is called "back".
It is what keeps a spinning motor from drawing huge current.
Imagine pushing a playground merry-go-round with a friend who runs along the rim. At the start, the merry-go-round is still, so you push hard.
As it speeds up, it moves away from your hand, and you can push less and less. The faster it goes, the less your push matters.
Back-EMF works the same way: speed reduces the net push of the supply. The analogy has one gap: the motor creates this opposition itself.
The two curves add to the supply at every speed. At stall the red curve is the whole 12 volts (maximum current).
As speed rises the back-EMF takes over and the resistive drop (hence current) shrinks. The slope is K e : steeper means a higher-voltage, lower-speed motor.
EMF: electromotive force, a voltage produced by a source. Here the source is the spinning coil. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, opposing the supply.
It equals K e omega : speed times a fixed number for each motor, K e . omega (omega): shaft speed in radians per second. One full turn is about 6. 28 radians.
Stall: shaft held still, so back-EMF is zero. Flyback voltage: a different effect, the spike when coil current is interrupted.
Take a 12 volts motor with a 1 ohms winding. Suppose K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s. Stalled, back-EMF is 0 volts, so the current is 12 volts / 1 ohms = 12 amps.
At 300 rad/s, back-EMF is 0. 02 times 300 = 6 volts. The net voltage is 12 minus 6 = 6 volts, so the current is 6 amps . At 575 rad/s, back-EMF is 11.
5 volts, so the current is only 0. 5 amps. That is the whole idea: faster spin means more back-EMF and less current.
"Back-EMF is the voltage a spinning motor generates: a coil moving in a magnetic field induces a voltage proportional to speed, e equals K e omega, and by Lenz's law it opposes the supply.
So the current is V minus back-EMF over R: huge at stall, small at speed, and voltage essentially sets speed while current sets torque.
It also gives free speed information for sensorless control and is what makes regenerative braking possible.
It's different from flyback voltage, which is the spike from interrupting the coil current."
